item.title: Packet Interval Modulation-based NFC for Scalable IoT around Meandered E-textile
item.description: arXiv:2610.35870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near-field communication (NFC) sensor tags are promising for low-cost, scalable environmental monitoring due to their battery-free, maintenance-free operation. Recent advances in NFC reader garments, integrated with conductive textile coils, allow users to interact seamlessly with tags scattered across their daily environment. However, dynamically identifying and reading out a fluctuating number of tags remains challenging. If multiple tags speak and collide, they must randomly retry until an empty slot is found. Standard NFC identifies tags using time-slotted ALOHA, which assigns tags to fixed time slots. If multiple tags speak and collide, they must retry with a tag filter to avoid collision until all tags are identified. This rigid setup is fragile in dynamic settings; as tags enter and leave the communication range, the heavy overhead of slot re-negotiation and inevitable collisions restricts data throughput. Here, we propose an asynchronous NFC based on packet interval modulation. By treating minimal ID-only packets as pulses and encoding data in their intervals, we enable communication through silence. This ensures the channel remains mostly unoccupied, drastically reducing collisions even in high-density environments. Our simulations show that for ten tags, our method achieves a 4-fold increase in throughput compared to the ALOHA approach. Furthermore, the system remains robust, maintaining over 160 bps/tag throughput even under extreme fluctuations in the number of tags over 20.
item.dc:creator: Shigemi Ishida, Ryo Takahashi, Satoshi Ido

item.title: Real-Time Smart Retail Analytics through Fog Computing using the RetailLightNet Lightweight Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.35871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart retail systems now depend on the application of real-time video analytics, which can track customer behavior, manage shelf inventory, and enhance in-store processes. Currently cloud-based applications of video analytics face multiple challenges such as high latency of the communication itself, privacy concerns surrounding transmitting raw video, and the computational demands of the heavy vision models used on the often limited network infrastructure. These challenges lead to delays in decision making where prompt action is crucial. To address these short comings, this research proposes Fog-based analytics withRetailLightNet (F RLN), an ultra lightweight deep learning model which is specifically suited for the edge, resource constrained hardware capabilities of devices like the NVIDIA Jetson Nano. The approach utilizes publicly available retail datasets, SKU110K, and RPC, which contains an assortment of product, shelf, and customer interaction scenarios for training.The processes include preprocessing images through normalization and employing motion-gated frame selection to improve efficiency by omitting redundant frames to ease the workload on the fog processing. Internal within Retail LightNet, image feature extraction is realized through depth wise separable convolutions which help support spatial and channel-wise learning without heavy computational costs. The model employs two prediction heads presence classification, and density regression, supporting shelf monitoring and queue assessment. The proposed F RLN framework attained better results in terms of precision (0.988), recall (0.976), and F1-score(0.976) when compared with existing convolutional neural network. Keywords: fog computing, motion-gated frame selection,NVIDIA jetson, retail lightnet, smart retail.
item.dc:creator: Mayank Atreya, Navin Chhibber, Shilpa Ajay, R Loshini, K Anitha

item.title: NSB2: An Open-Source Modular Pipeline for Application-Network Co-Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As connected applications -- from intelligence-enabled assistants and the smart homes to autonomous vehicles and large-scale Internet-of-Things deployments -- become increasingly pervasive, their performance, safety, and reliability depend more than ever on the underlying network. Designing and validating such systems therefore requires development environments that holistically account for both application and network behavior. While network simulators and emulators provide high-fidelity models of network behavior, connecting full-fledged applications to them remains difficult due to platform constraints, simulator-specific interfaces, and narrow single-purpose integrations. To address this gap, we present NSB2 (Network Simulation Bridge 2), an open-source network co-simulation middleware that relays payloads between application processes through a network simulator. NSB2 is composed of a central daemon and thin, embedded application- and simulator-side libraries for flexible integration, disentangled communication channels for unencumbered inter-process communications, and in-memory key-value storage for efficient payload caching and retrieval. NSB2 is designed to be lightweight, accessible, and extensible: it exposes streamlined interfaces supported in Python and C++, modular internal abstractions that let users swap or extend network simulation/emulation backends, flexible and configurable deployment modes, and integration helpers for the widely-used ns-3 and OMNeT++ network simulators. Our evaluation across multiple co-simulation scenarios shows that NSB2 introduces negligible memory and latency overhead, enabling researchers and developers to achieve richer, more realistic modeling of connected systems with minimum overhead.
item.dc:creator: Harikrishna Kuttivelil, Lakshmi Krishnaswamy, Srikar Rani, Psi Padhya, Alex Woelkers, Vasavi Doddamani, Nayan Bhatia, Katia Obraczka

item.title: IoT-based Smart Real-Time Energy-Aware Server Room Monitoring System
item.description: arXiv:2610.35873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) into monitoring systems has become increasingly significant across various fields, including energy management, environmental monitoring, and industrial applications. This paper proposes a smart, real-time, energy-aware monitoring system architecture for IoT using a brokerless Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware. Environmental and electrical metrics are transmitted with high reliability, achieving an average latency of 1.76 milliseconds and a throughput of 57.1 Mbps. These metrics are processed by a multi-head Long Short-Term Memory network. Evaluated on the empirical TDC2.0 data center dataset, the architecture simultaneously performs three tasks: predicting thermal stress, detecting cooling inefficiency, and forecasting multi-step cooling power demand. The multi task network achieved an F1-score of 0.92 for proactive thermal stress prediction and demonstrated the capability to identify systemic cooling anomalies. Furthermore, the model generated consistent power forecasts across 5-minute, 10-minute, and 30 minute horizons, maintaining an R2 > 0.83. A post-hoc SHAP analysis indicated that the predictive logic aligns with established thermodynamic relationships. Overall, the proposed architecture offers a transparent and low-latency framework for critical facility management.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Dikko Gambo, Sami Ul Haq, Syed M. Minhaj Naqvi, Khaled M. Rabie, Abdallah Moubayed

item.title: Where Does My Call Go? Measuring Google Meet, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams on Starlink
item.description: arXiv:2610.35874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellite networks are expanding broadband access, but major Real-Time Communication (RTC) platforms, including Google Meet, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams, still rely on service-point selection mechanisms that appear to be largely shaped by terrestrial-network assumptions. As a result, they may not consistently account for LEO-specific dynamics such as satellite topology and Point-of-Presence (PoP) changes, especially during in-flight connectivity. To characterize RTC service-point selection over Starlink, we measure RTC performance using a Canada-wide testbed and more than 24 hours of in-flight experiments. Our results show clear platform differences. Google Meet tends to align more closely with the serving PoP, consistent with broader observed edge coverage. Zoom follows a regional service-point selection pattern, while Microsoft Teams often remains tied to fixed service points. Moreover, we show that in-flight PoP handovers can shift traffic egress points mid-session, and that RTC platforms respond differently to these changes. In some cases, this interaction leads to suboptimal service-point selections and RTT inflation. Overall, our findings suggest that LEO connectivity can expose mismatches between Starlink egress dynamics and RTC service-point selection, motivating further measurement and LEO-optimized designs for service placement and selection.
item.dc:creator: Kousar Malekinasab, Mostafa Abdollah, Jinwei Zhao, Jianping Pan

item.title: ML-OLLA: Link Adaptation for Real-Time Traffic in 5G/6G NTN Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.36147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable low-latency connectivity for real-time applications is a key requirement for 5G and future 6G non-terrestrial networks. Low Earth Orbit satellites enable global coverage but impose long propagation delays, rapid channel variations, and delayed feedback, which challenge conventional link adaptation algorithms designed for terrestrial networks. To address this problem, the paper proposes a Multi-Level Outer-Loop Link Adaptation (ML-OLLA) algorithm that assigns a dedicated target block error rate and an independent adaptation process for each transmission attempt. With ML-OLLA, early transmission attempts use higher-rate modulation and coding schemes (MCSs), while later ones use more robust MCSs. The core contribution of this work is a low-complexity data-driven parameter selection method that determines ML-OLLA parameters. Numerical results obtained with ns-3 show that the proposed ML-OLLA algorithm increases the system capacity by up to four times and reduces the minimum supported latency budget. In particular, for the 99.9% reliability target, ML-OLLA reduces the minimum supported latency budget from 60 ms to 40 ms compared with the baseline OLLA.
item.dc:creator: Artur Magamedov, Artem Krasilov, Roman Zlobin, Evgeny Khorov

item.title: Adaptive Calibration of RF Digital Twins via Budget-Constrained Radio Measurement Selection
item.description: arXiv:2610.36406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) digital twins (DTs) enable site-specific wireless propagation prediction by explicitly reconstructing the physical environment and modeling electromagnetic interactions. Although physics-based DTs reduce reliance on exhaustive measurements, systematic bias relative to real radio data arises from environmental uncertainty, material inaccuracies, and geometric abstractions. Calibration using field measurements is therefore necessary but costly under limited sampling budgets. This paper studies active RF DT calibration, in which measurement locations are selected sequentially and in an online manner to estimate a calibration offset under strict measurement budget constraints. A physics-based RF DT pipeline is developed, integrating semantic geospatial data from OpenStreetMap, 3D modeling in Blender, and deterministic ray tracing in Sionna to capture dominant building and foliage effects. This RF DT is calibrated using path-loss measurements collected with software-defined radios. Multiple online calibration strategies that select radio measurement locations are compared, including random sampling, rank-structured sampling with balanced coverage, quasi-Monte Carlo ranked selection, progressive structure-aware allocation, and fully adaptive uncertainty-driven sampling with estimator stabilization. Results demonstrate that adaptive and structure-aware schemes significantly improve both mean and worst-case calibration accuracy, particularly in the low-budget regime for radio measurements.
item.dc:creator: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Hossein Jafari

item.title: Martingale-Based Resource Partitioning Bounds for URLLC and eMBB Network Slicing in 5G
item.description: arXiv:2610.36602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network slicing is a key enabler for the coexistence of ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC) and enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) in 5G networks. However, allocating limited radio resources to heterogeneous slices while satisfying stringent quality-of-service (QoS) requirements remains challenging, particularly in the ultra-reliable regime where conventional effective-capacity-based approaches may lead to excessive resource allocation. To address this issue, this paper proposes a martingale-based resource block (RB) allocation framework for coexisting URLLC and eMBB slices. By constructing exponential martingale processes using the moment generating functions (MGFs) of the arrival and service processes and applying Doob's maximal inequality, explicit non-asymptotic upper bounds are derived for the URLLC delay violation probability and the eMBB backlog violation probability. Based on the resulting theoretical stability conditions, a low-complexity bisection algorithm is developed to determine the optimal martingale parameters, followed by a deterministic search algorithm to obtain the minimum RB requirements for both slices. Numerical results show that the analytical bounds effectively upper-bound the Monte Carlo simulation results. At a target violation probability of $10^{-6}$ for each slice, the proposed framework requires 44 RBs in total, satisfying the system capacity constraint of 50 RBs. Compared with the conventional effective-capacity baseline requiring 64 RBs, the proposed framework reduces total RB consumption by approximately 31.2% relative to the conventional effective-capacity baseline.
item.dc:creator: Hanbing Li, Yantong Wang

item.title: RadarCom: Unlocking Simultaneous Communication and Sensing on Commodity Automotive mmWave Radars
item.description: arXiv:2610.36622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication can improve road safety and traffic efficiency, yet its deployment remains limited by the need for dedicated communication hardware and supporting infrastructure. Meanwhile, production vehicles are already widely equipped with millimeter-wave radars for sensing. To unlock their communication potential, this paper presents RadarCom, a software-defined system that enables direct radar-to-radar communication on unmodified commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) automotive mmWave radars while preserving their native sensing functionality. The key insight is that mutual inter-radar interference, traditionally viewed as harmful, can be repurposed as a communication carrier. Based on this insight, RadarCom introduces slope-mismatch-based discovery, adaptive chirp synchronization, differential coding on range-FFT, and sensing-aware interference suppression to enable simultaneous communication and sensing without hardware modification, waveform redesign, or infrastructure support. We implement RadarCom on TI AWR2243 automotive radars and evaluate it under static, dynamic, and challenging real-world conditions. Results show an average effective data rate of 5.55 kbps with symbol error rates below 1.5%, while maintaining sensing F1 scores of up to 80.5% during concurrent communication. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transforming commodity automotive radars into dual-purpose communication and sensing devices.
item.dc:creator: Yi Wei, Yue Zhang, Peijun Hou, Qiuyu Liao, Nan Cen

item.title: Axiom: a logic programming language to express and enforce network designs
item.description: arXiv:2610.36748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human errors remain the leading cause of network outages. To prevent them researchers propose general verifiers that analyze the network behavior. Yet, their (symbolic) models struggle to accurately reflect network devices, they fail to scale to large networks, and report misbehavior, not what configuration line caused it. We attribute all three challenges to specifications that describe the intended behavior but not how operators intend to achieve it---the network's design: which protocols to run and how to combine them. We present Axiom, a language for expressing network designs, and a checker that finds every violation and the responsible commands. Operators state their design decision as rules over configuration commands. Axiom then compiles them into a single Datalog program that checks the entire network directly on its configurations, not on the state they produce. Our prototype checks a 754-router network within seconds. Ultimately, a design enforced on every keystroke could give network operators the integrated development environment that programmers have long enjoyed.
item.dc:creator: Tibor Schneider, Laurent Vanbever

item.title: Sample-and-Score: Surrogate-Guided Coordinated Spatial Reuse in IEEE 802.11 Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.36868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coordinated spatial reuse (Co-SR) in IEEE 802.11bn increases area throughput through simultaneous transmissions, yet the combinatorial configuration space makes real-time optimization challenging. We propose a sample-and-score approach: draw random Co-SR configurations, score each with a surrogate model, and select the best. The surrogate is trained offline and deployed without online fine-tuning or sequential exploration, yet performs close to multi-armed bandit and heuristic baselines that need multiple interaction steps or extensive measurements. On unseen topologies with 2-16 access points, it recovers 52-77% of a perfect surrogate's throughput. A perfect sample-and-score approach reaches 95% of the upper bound throughput with 8192 candidates.
item.dc:creator: Maksymilian Wojnar

item.title: OFDM-Based Neuromorphic Wake-Up Signal
item.description: arXiv:2610.36914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wake-up radios (WURs) reduce energy consumption by continuously monitoring the channel for a wake-up signal (WUS) while the main receiver remains asleep. Neuromorphic computing offers a promising approach to ultra-low-power WUS detection through sparse, event-driven processing. However, realizing these benefits requires spike-like inputs, which conventional orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) waveforms do not naturally provide. To enable neuromorphic WUS detection in OFDM-based systems, we introduce a neuromorphic wake-up signal (nWUS) that can be generated by a standard OFDM transmitter. The proposed design superposes frequency-domain vectors with linear phase progressions across the OFDM subcarriers, producing a time-domain waveform with sparse amplitude peaks at predefined positions. These peaks encode the wake-up signature in a spike-like representation that facilitates neuromorphic processing at the receiver. Building on this structure, we then propose a noncoherent neuromorphic detector that encodes received peaks into spikes and performs sparse correlation only upon spike events. Simulations over a 3GPP urban macro channel show that the proposed approach outperforms on-off keying (OOK) baselines in detection probability while achieving up to 43.5x lower computational cost. During idle periods, event-driven processing further reduces correlation operations by 86% relative to nWUS reception.
item.dc:creator: Gaspard Goupy, Elias Raninen, Dani Korpi

item.title: From Ethernet to Wi-Fi: Flow Feature Selection and Construction for Traffic Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.37007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-based traffic classifiers trained on Ethernet data may lose accuracy when applied to Wi-Fi traffic. This paper proposes a five-stage procedure for selecting and constructing features that enable Wi-Fi flow classification using models trained only on Ethernet data. The procedure removes the transport protocol identifier, examines rate dependence, compares feature distributions and the information each feature provides for the application classes, reduces redundancy, and constructs normalized packet-size and temporal features. Ethernet and Wi-Fi traffic are simulated in ns-3, with Wi-Fi using Best Effort access category. Labelled Wi-Fi data from six development scenarios are used for feature design, while a separate scenario is reserved for final testing. The evaluation compares feature sets, examines threshold sensitivity, and analyses classification errors under different traffic conditions.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Rau, Petia Georgieva, Carlos Herranz, I\~naki Val, Joaquin Perez

item.title: MAPLE-Sec: Mobility-Aware Partitioned Language-Model Engine for Roaming IoT Security
item.description: arXiv:2610.37147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile Internet-of-Things (IoT) endpoints such as connected vehicles, wearables, and drones continuously cross heterogeneous network domains, creating handover-driven attack surfaces that static, cloud-anchored detectors cannot follow. However, three obstacles block real-time detection on such roaming endpoints: detection state is lost at every inter-domain handover; transmitting raw telemetry to a fixed detector exhausts the uplink and the device battery; and full-depth language model inference cannot meet millisecond latency budgets on constrained hardware. To tackle these challenges, we propose MAPLE-Sec, a mobility-aware partitioning framework that splits a compact, security-tuned language model across a roaming device and its nearest edge node. First, a trajectory-conditioned partition scheduler recomputes the split point from predicted handover timing, residual battery, and uplink quality. Second, a token-budgeted early-exit mechanism emits a verdict at the shallowest layer that meets a confidence threshold. Finally, a learned activation-compression codec migrates the intermediate inference state across edge nodes during handover without retransmitting raw telemetry. We formalize the partition-and-migration decision as an on-device constrained optimization solved in sub-millisecond time. Extensive experiments across the CIC-IoT and Edge-IIoTset corpora under both IID and non-IID roaming conditions demonstrate that MAPLE-Sec sustains detection across mobility events, improving the converged F1-score by up to 9.3\% relative to Cloud-only and by 2.9 percentage points over the strongest edge-collaborative baseline (EdgeShard), while reducing end-to-end latency by up to 2.5$\times$. Ablation confirms that the activation-compression codec reduces migration energy by 2.4$\times$ versus the raw-activation migration variant.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Qiu, Ziwei Li, Jinfeng Xu, Jialiang Xie, Fangmin Ren, Shirong Guo, Jing Yang, Sunil Prajapat, Por Lip Yee

item.title: Keeping Inference in the Radio: Design and Measurement of a Spiking Accelerator for mmWave ISAC Activity Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2610.37480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication allows wireless networks to recognize human activity from the channel estimates that the receiver computes anyway. The inference, however, runs on the general-purpose processors of the base station, access point or handset, which are the first components a device switches off to save energy. Always-on sensing therefore requires a classifier that is small enough to remain powered while the rest of the system sleeps. We investigate whether Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) can provide such a classifier. To this end, we generate SNN accelerators for micro-Doppler activity recognition on the public DISC dataset (IEEE 802.11ay at 60 GHz) with the open-source Spiker+ framework, and implement them together with a spike encoder on a ZCU208 RFSoC, so that the complete chain from micro-Doppler frame to activity label runs in programmable logic. A fully connected SNN with 132 neurons achieves 94.7 % accuracy (90.7 % macro-F1) on unseen subjects and performs an inference in 206 microseconds. Compared to conventional networks of the same topology on the same device, it requires an eighth of the logic and 3.4X less dynamic energy per decision than a network fed the same binary spikes, at comparable accuracy, and 7.6X less than a network fed the 16-bit spectrogram, at 1.2 points lower accuracy. Quantization-aware training reduces its weights to 3 bits within half a percentage point of the 6-bit network at the same encoder threshold
item.dc:creator: Anthony S\'anchez, Rafael Ruiz, Jos\'e A. Belloch, Jes\'us O. Lacruz, Joerg Widmer

item.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
item.description: arXiv:2610.36631v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.
item.dc:creator: Adam Visokay, Soumyakanti Pan, Molly Griston, Polina Iasakova, Mark Nepf, Denis Peskoff, Riya Sinha, Jikai Sun, Isabelle Thiara, Letao Wang, Yiwei Wu, Lauren Yan, Tyler H. McCormick

item.title: Where to Sample: Rethinking ML-Based Malicious Traffic Detection at Terabit Scale
item.description: arXiv:2403.18788v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine Learning (ML)-based malicious traffic detectors can identify unseen attacks, including in encrypted traffic, but scaling them to Terabit rates remains challenging. Packet sampling, commonly used to meet processing limits, can discard essential behavioral information and render detection ineffective. We present Peregrine, a hardware-software co-designed architecture built around a simple principle: compute features before sampling. Peregrine updates ML features over all traffic at line rate in a programmable switch, then downsamples the feature records sent to software inference. We instantiate this design with two detectors that impose distinct feature-computation requirements on the switch. Across 84 attack traces from three datasets, we show that approximate features computed over all packets can outperform exact features computed from sampled packets. In our evaluation, Peregrine preserves detection effectiveness while reducing feature-record rates by three orders of magnitude - even where pre-feature sampling causes detection to collapse.
item.dc:creator: Jo\~ao Romeiras Amado, Francisco Pereira, David Pissarra, Salvatore Signorello, Miguel Correia, Fernando M. V. Ramos

item.title: GLo-MAPPO: Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Energy-Efficient UAV-Assisted LoRa Networks
item.description: arXiv:2509.17676v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid advancement of Low-Power Wide Area Networks (LPWANs), particularly Long Range (LoRa) technology, has positioned them as a cornerstone of Next-Generation Internet of Things (NG-IoT) applications. Despite their long-range and low-power advantages, achieving high energy efficiency (EE) in LoRa networks remains a significant challenge in highly dynamic environments. Traditional terrestrial gateway deployments often suffer from coverage gaps and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) propagation, while satellite-based alternatives incur excessive energy consumption and prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we propose a multi-UAV architecture in which unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) serve as mobile LoRa gateways to dynamically collect data from LoRa end devices (EDs). We formulate a joint optimization problem to maximize the weighted system EE by jointly optimizing spreading factors, transmission powers, UAV trajectories, and ED-UAV associations. This problem is transformed into a partially observable stochastic game (POSG), which we solve using our proposed Green LoRa Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (GLo-MAPPO). We adopt PPO because its clipped surrogate objective discourages excessively large policy updates, thereby promoting stable learning as multiple UAV agents simultaneously adapt their behaviors. Combined with centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE), this enables coordinated policy learning while allowing each UAV to make decisions independently during execution. Simulation results show that GLo-MAPPO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) benchmarks in terms of EE and power consumption across varying network densities. We further validate the trained policy through closed-loop, packet-level co-simulation using the OMNeT++/FLoRa LoRa simulator. Finally, ....
item.dc:creator: Abdullahi Isa Ahmed, Jamal Bentahar, El Mehdi Amhoud

item.title: DeGenTWeb: A First Look at MGT-dominant Websites
item.description: arXiv:2605.00087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many news reports have claimed that machine-generated text (MGT) from large language models (LLMs) is taking over the web. However, these claims are typically not based on a representative sample of the web, and the methodology underlying them is often opaque. Consequently, we lack an understanding of the true prevalence and characteristics of MGT on the web. We describe DeGenTWeb, which systematically identifies MGT-dominant websites: sites whose informational prose content is mostly MGT, with little human input. We show how to adapt detectors of MGT for use on web pages, and how to aggregate detection results from multiple pages on a site for accurate site-level categorization. DeGenTWeb mislabels only 0.12% of human-authored sites as MGT-dominant. We find that 20.9% of the sites archived by Common Crawl between January and July 2026 and 13.6% of the sites linked from Bing's search results in 2025 are MGT-dominant. These figures are lower bounds on the prevalence of MGT-dominant sites. We also find that the fraction of MGT-dominant sites is growing over time, and that many such sites share the same owner. We will release all of our code and data after publication.
item.dc:creator: Sichang Steven He, Calvin Ardi, Ramesh Govindan, Harsha V. Madhyastha

item.title: Kom8ndor: An IEEE 802.11bn-Oriented Simulator for Wi-Fi 8 and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2606.25435v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The upcoming IEEE 802.11bn amendment marks a paradigm shift in Wi-Fi, which will pose ambitious performance targets under the paradigm of Ultra-High Reliability (UHR). To understand the implications of such a new technology and to support early research and protocol design for Wi-Fi 8, we present Kom8ndor. This discrete-event network simulator extends the open-source Komondor platform (a simulator validated against ns-3 and other analytical tools) with 802.11bn features. Among the newly added functionalities, we highlight Multi-Access Point Coordination (MAPC)-including Coordinated Time-Division Multiple Access (Co-TDMA), Coordinated Spatial Reuse (Co-SR), and Coordinated Beamforming (Co-BF)-, Non-Primary Channel Access (NPCA), and Dynamic Subband Operation (DSO). Beyond Wi-Fi 8 implementations, Kom8ndor introduces novel functionalities (e.g., a machine learning wrapper for building AI-based protocols) and a modular design to boost the prototyping and research of future Wi-Fi technologies. Kom8ndor is open-source (GNU GPLv3) and available at https://github.com/wn-upf/Komondor.
item.dc:creator: Francesc Wilhelmi, Sergio Barrachina-Mu\~noz, Boris Bellalta

item.title: NetGuise: Adversarial Traffic Generation for Early-Stage Classifier Evasion
item.description: arXiv:2610.27456v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Early-stage encrypted traffic classifiers make decisions from only the first few packets of a connection, enabling low-latency classification but raising robustness concerns under realistic traffic morphing. Existing adversarial traffic generation methods often assume complete flows, feature-level perturbations, or iterative runtime feedback, which do not match the constraints of early-stage execution. We present NetGuise, a target-conditioned traffic morphing framework that generates packet-level padding and non-negative delay actions while preserving packet direction, ordering, and packet count and respecting MTU, bandwidth, and latency constraints. We evaluate NetGuise for censorship evasion under two observation interfaces, i) a history-only causal interface for online packet-by-packet execution, ii) and a full-window oracle interface that provides an upper-bound characterization of early-stage morphability. On VANT, NetGuise achieves 33.2% mean targeted evasion under the causal interface versus 82.0% under the oracle interface; on UTMobileNet, the corresponding results are 5.6% and 81.8%. NetGuise outperforms the strongest causal baseline, BAP, on both datasets and, on VANT, reduces bandwidth overhead from 19.80% to 3.02% and generation latency from 37.42 ms/flow to 1.16 ms/flow. Under the oracle interface, it achieves up to 85.7% targeted evasion, retains 43.5% after four rounds of adaptive censor retraining, and maintains 48% under zero-shot cross-environment transfer. Our results show that early-stage classifiers can remain morphable despite high clean accuracy and that robustness evaluation should account for targeted morphability, observation constraints, defender adaptation, and operational network conditions.
item.dc:creator: Binghui Wu, Dinil Mon Divakaran, Mohan Gurusamy

item.title: 5uGUE: Agentic Hardware-in-the-Loop Fuzzing for 5G Devices and beyond
item.description: arXiv:2610.29155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we present 5uGUE, a large language model (LLM)-driven hardware-in-the-loop agent, which enables the wireless fuzzing of 5G-enabled devices (such as mobile phones). 5uGUE combines multi-step reasoning with tool-assisted interaction and integrates into the fuzzing pipeline by leveraging specialized tools for internet search, 5G protocol analysis, memory management, and test-case execution. The agent iteratively generates test cases, executes them on targets, collects runtime feedback, and adaptively refines the fuzzing strategy. We evaluate 5uGUE on five commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) 5G devices across six LLMs. The best performing runs for 5uGUE trigger 167 crashes in total (141 novel and 31 unique) within 60 interaction turns (49 to 133 minutes total runtime). In contrast, the best runs for the state-of-the-art baseline (5GHOUL) discovers only 13 crashes in total (10 novel and 6 unique) within 150 minutes. Overall, by integrating LLM-driven agents, 5uGUE demonstrates significantly better crash discovery performance (12.8x total, 5.2x unique improvement). Notably, our experiments identified 46 unique crashes, 44 of which were confirmed by the vendors but had been previously reported. More importantly, MediaTek confirmed two previously unknown, high-severity vulnerabilities, one of which was assigned CVE-2026-20525. Finally, to demonstrate that 5uGUE is agnostic to wireless protocols, we also extend it to Bluetooth Classic with only minimal code changes. In our evaluations, 5uGUE finds an average of 6.4 novel crashes and 1.6 unique crashes. In a nutshell, 5uGUE highlights that LLM agents are capable to operate effectively beyond software-in-the-loop settings, extending autonomous vulnerability discovery to the proprietary, hardware-bound systems that affect billions of end-user devices across multiple wireless protocols.

item.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
item.description: arXiv:2610.34554v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80{\deg}S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.
item.dc:creator: Christopher J. Santorelli, Alexander M. Wyglinski

item.title: R2CC: Reliable and Resilient Collective Communication for Distributed Learning
item.description: arXiv:2512.25059v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern ML training and inference now span hundreds to tens of thousands of GPUs, where failures can waste 10-15% of GPU hours due to slow recovery. Common network errors and link fluctuations can cause up to 50% of job interruptions, triggering timeouts that often terminate entire jobs, forcing expensive checkpoint rollback during training and request reprocessing during inference. We present R2CC, a fault-tolerant communication library that provides lossless, low-overhead failover by exploiting multi-NIC hardware. R2CC performs rapid connection migration, bandwidth-aware load redistribution, and resilient collective algorithms to maintain progress under failures. We evaluate R2CC on four 8-GPU H100 InfiniBand servers and via large-scale ML simulators modeling up to 1024 GPUs with diverse failure patterns. Experiments show that R2CC is highly robust to inter-node network failures, incurring less than 1.1% training and 3% inference overhead under active failure scenarios. Compared to existing fault-tolerant approaches, R2CC reduces failure-induced overhead by up to 92% for training and 98% for inference. R2CC is open-sourced at https://github.com/r2cc-project/R2CC.
item.dc:creator: Wei Wang, Nengneng Yu, Sixian Xiong, Zaoxing Liu

item.title: Domain Decoupling Attack: Exploiting the Validation Gap Between Protective DNS and Shared Edge Routing
item.description: arXiv:2608.00643v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Command-and-control, data transfer, and censorship circumvention can hide in traffic to widely used services. DNS-bound access control grants permits based on resolved IP addresses, while shared edges route requests by tenant identity, creating a validation gap. An attacker can resolve an allowed anchor, obtain a permit for its shared edge address, and access a hidden tenant by presenting the tenant's name as both SNI and HTTP Host. To investigate this gap, we present the Domain Decoupling Attack (DDA), which exploits this gap in CDN and non-CDN hosting while preserving SNI--Host consistency. Across 1,069,048 domains, we conduct 18,025,068 successful probes. Overall, 95.8% of domains accept an external SNI, and 84.6% return content matching the named tenant. Exposure reaches 99.26% across 506,763 CDN domains and 92.75% across 562,285 non-CDN domains. The co-location graph places 666,413 exposed domains in cross-tenant components; 97.7% of 54,069 cross-tenant non-CDN addresses have a confirmed path to another tenant. None of the tested defenses bind tenant identity to the DNS-approved name. Cleartext inline IPS can block access based on SNI, but Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides it. The Windows Zero Trust DNS (ZTDNS) permit remains reusable in both cases, enabling the concealment of command-and-control and data-exfiltration traffic and facilitating censorship circumvention. The risk conceals command-and-control and data-exfiltration traffic and supports censorship.
item.dc:creator: Weizhe Wang, Minhong Dong, Jinhao Li, Lyuchuan Wei, Yao Zhang, Qiang Hu, Qi Guo, Guangquan Xu, Bin Wu
